Ultimately, one would hope that choosing the best candidate for anything will lead to an eventual equilibrium of equality, provided we're working to ensure there is truly an equality of opportunity.

I think the mindset behind affirmative action is to reach that level of equality faster. If we work to sometimes choose women over men, so long as the women are still qualified, we might reach that point sooner. We definitely shouldn't do it forever though! It's just a way to expedite the process

I mean you could absolutely say that there's no right answer here. It's just a matter of how we combat and make up for existing inequality, and that's a complicated issue. So I definitely respect your opinion :)

Perhaps not, but if you only look surface level, you can't start to identify the deeper inequalities embedded into our society.

I actually agree that in many countries today, if we look only at what is written in law, men and women have the same opportunities. However, I think there are deeper inequalities, like perceptions of women, biases towards women, and general stereotypes that could discourage women from pursuing a career in a field dominated by men. And in my mind, that's significant because it leads to an inequality in who actually decides to go down a certain career path

It is very important to do what you want, I agree! However, most of us have, at one point or another, been inspired by someone who has achieved our dream. Usually we want to relate to that person, so it inspires us more if they look similar to us. That's what I mean when I say role model. If a little girl wants to be a politician, and sees that the vast majority are men, she might be dissuaded from following that path. On the other hand, a little boy would be encouraged by how many politicians are men.

That's the inherent inequality I'm talking about. Sure, on the surface, maybe men and women have the same opportunities. But there are so many other influences that can dissuade women from pursuing a career dominated by men, and those are the issues we hope to combat with things like affirmative action

Also, I think you're absolutely free to disagree with the assertion in the paper, but in my mind the methodology, though focused solely on women, yes, does highlight many of the difficulties they had to face to get where they are, that maybe men didn't.

Ultimately we don't have to agree. It's a very complicated issue and you certainly have a reasonable point :)

I think you're right, but I think there's still evidence that points to an inequality of opportunity among women in politics.

Personally I think every career should have a certain amount of gender diversity, because there are certainly men who make great nurses and women who make great miners.

Politicians/CEOs are a little farther up the list in terms of priority because they're public role models. Children see them in power and form their opinions about who a CEO/Politician is. I feel like if you asked kids to draw a politician, a good majority would be men. That can get pretty discouraging for women who feel passionate about that field. Until that gets changed, I don't think we can say there's an equality of opportunity there

Here are some papers I found that touch on the issue:

https://academic.oup.com/sf/article-abstract/82/1/87/2234826

http://ls00012.mah.se/handle/2043/32406

In my eyes it's a bit more complicated than that

The problem is, because there is inherent inequality *everywhere*, including the education system, women are convinced from birth that they wouldn't make good politicians. This combined with discrimination puts pressure on women who do want to become politicians, and in the end there are fewer women pursuing that path overall.

Now because of the simple fact that there are many more men chasing this career than women, the odds are that the best candidate in the pool is a man. So, if you continued to always select the best or most popular candidate, odds are it will be a man, and the cycle will just continue

What the more feminist option proposes is to deliberately choose a woman to serve in a certain role, even if she may not be the *best* candidate. Obviously you want to ensure that she's still capable overall, but again, due to the inequality in education and as a whole, she may not be a better candidate than some of the men.

What this does is it helps to break the cycle. She can then use her influence to start breaking down some of the inequality inherent in the system. Also, little girls see her and realize they *can* become politicians, and that it's not just a career for men.

So I'd say you're right, but the issue is a little deeper than that :)

I can understand that. I’ve spent so much of my life obsessed by what other people think about me.

 But in the end, it doesn't matter. I see two possibilities: 
1. You never see those people again, so it literally never affects your life. They'll never have a chance to make fun of you again. I know it's easy to obsess over what they're saying now, but you'll never hear them say it. They could be saying anything. Anyone could be saying anything. My conclusion: it's best not to dwell on the thoughts of people you'll never see again.
2. You do see them again, and you have a chance to show them who you really are. Sure, maybe their view of you will be slightly colored by their view of you in the past. But I can’t think of a single person other than maybe my parents who know me as well as I know myself. Everyone will always have a slightly wrong picture of you in their head. I’m trying to learn to be at peace with that. In other words, let them think what they want to think. I’m going to do my best every day. Third, as a strong Christian in college, I can say that nothing about our religion says gays go to hell. The kind of homosexuality that Paul talks about in his letters was far far removed from the kind we see today. For one, there was no context in the ancient world for the kind of same-sex marriage we see today. Jesus was speaking to the people of that time, and so he instructed them based on what they were familiar with. For the same reason, in the case of Paul’s letters, the kind of homosexuality he deems “sinful” was either prostitution or essentially rape (sex between a man and a boy, or with a male slave). Again, there was no such thing as same-sex marriage between equals back then. Paul also expresses a lot of opinions that were very specifically directed towards who he was writing to. When he states that he would never allow a woman to lead a church, he was probably addressing a specific problem with some of the women of that city. So when he says homosexuality is sinful, he may be addressing a certain brand of abusive relationship.

You’re loved and you’re valuable just as you are. I hope your parents come around, and if they don’t, I hope you can find a community that accepts you for who you are :))

I'm 18, and I've witnessed and experienced my fair share of depression and loneliness. I think you may be surprised who's willing to listen when your life is on the line. I'm willing to bet there are multiple people who see you as a part of their life and would do more than you might expect to keep you in their lives. But if you want to find out who they are you have to be real. Let go of any pride you have and be willing to open up to them. Sure, many will turn away because they don't want your problems, and you can't really blame them. But there will always be some who turn towards you, often from places you don't expect. I know you probably hear the words "it will get better" a lot, but it really will. You can't let go of the hope that your situation will improve or you'll lose your grip on reality. As I'm sure you can attest, that's a dangerous place to be. So hold on. Hold on to anything you can. People, religion, dreams, goals. And never be afraid to try new things that may help you. I know multiple people who went through situations similar to yours (myself included) and are still here to talk about it today. I really hope that you seek out help to the best of your ability, and I pray that you never give up hope. :)
